$$w=(X^{\top}X)^{-1}X^{\top}y$$

The model and its matrix forms

One feature, then two, then \(d\) — and the three equivalent ways of writing the same thing.

One feature

Ten houses, one predictor. We want a straight line through the cloud that sits as close to the points as possible.

$$\text{Price} = 1030.03 + 119.22 \times \text{SquareFootage}$$
SQUARE_FTPRICE

\(n = 10\) data points, \(d = 1\) feature.

Two features

Add the number of rooms. The line becomes a plane; everything else is unchanged.

$$\text{Price} = -15434.85 + 130.00 \times \text{SquareFootage} + 16788.50 \times \text{Rooms}$$

\(n = 10\), \(d = 2\).

The general form

The pattern extends without change. Each feature contributes a term, and one constant sits outside the sum:

$$\begin{aligned} \text{1 feature:}\quad & \hat y = w_0 + w_1 x_1\\[2pt] \text{2 features:}\quad & \hat y = w_0 + w_1 x_1 + w_2 x_2\\[2pt] \text{$k$ features:}\quad & \hat y = w_0 + w_1 x_1 + w_2 x_2 + \dots + w_k x_k \end{aligned}$$

Per data point \(i\), with \(n\) points and \(d\) features:

$$\hat y_i = w_0 + \sum_{j=1}^{d} w_j x_{i,j}, \qquad i = 1,2,\dots,n$$

Vector form

Stack all \(n\) predictions into a column and the whole dataset becomes one matrix product. Watch the shapes — they are the fastest way to catch an algebra mistake.

$$\underbrace{\hat y}_{n\times 1} \;=\; \underbrace{w_0}_{n\times 1} \;+\; \underbrace{X}_{n\times d}\;\underbrace{w}_{d\times 1}$$

Here \(X\) holds one row per data point and one column per feature; \(w_0\) is the same intercept repeated \(n\) times.

$$X=\begin{bmatrix} x_{1,1} & x_{1,2} & \cdots & x_{1,d}\\ x_{2,1} & x_{2,2} & \cdots & x_{2,d}\\ \vdots & \vdots & \ddots & \vdots \\ x_{n,1} & x_{n,2} & \cdots & x_{n,d} \end{bmatrix}, \qquad w=\begin{bmatrix} w_1\\ w_2\\ \vdots\\ w_d\end{bmatrix}$$

Augmented form

Carrying \(w_0\) separately is a nuisance. Glue a column of ones onto the front of \(X\) and put \(w_0\) at the top of \(w\). The intercept is then just another weight multiplying a feature that happens to always equal 1.

$$\underbrace{\begin{bmatrix} 1 & x_{1,1} & \cdots & x_{1,d}\\ 1 & x_{2,1} & \cdots & x_{2,d}\\ \vdots & \vdots & \ddots & \vdots\\ 1 & x_{n,1} & \cdots & x_{n,d} \end{bmatrix}}_{n\times(d+1)} \underbrace{\begin{bmatrix} w_0\\ w_1\\ \vdots\\ w_d\end{bmatrix}}_{(d+1)\times 1} \;=\;\underbrace{\hat y}_{n\times 1} \qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad \hat y = Xw$$

From here on, \(\hat y = Xw\) means the augmented version. Every formula in the rest of these notes assumes it.

Notation

\(y\) is the observed target from the data. \(\hat y\) is the predicted value the model produces. They are different vectors, and the gap between them is what we are about to minimise.

If \(n=10\) and \(d=3\), what are the shapes of \(X\), \(w\), \(\hat y\) and \(X^{\top}X\) in augmented form?

\(X\) is \(10\times 4\), \(w\) is \(4\times 1\), \(\hat y\) is \(10\times 1\), and \(X^{\top}X\) is \(4\times 4\). Note that \(X^{\top}X\) is always square with side equal to the number of weights, no matter how many data points you have.

2

Errors, loss functions, the OLS objective

What we measure, what a good measure has to satisfy, and why squared error wins.

The error vector

For each data point, the error is the vertical gap between what actually happened and what the model predicted:

$$\text{error}_i = y_i - \hat y_i$$

What a loss function should satisfy

Loss measures how well our prediction performs against the data. Before picking one, it helps to say what we want from it.

PropertyMeaning
Non-negativityLoss should never be negative: \(L(y,\hat y)\ge 0\)
Zero at perfection\(L(y,\hat y)=0\) when \(y=\hat y\)
Symmetry\(L(y,\hat y)=L(\hat y,y)\) — over- and under-prediction penalised alike
ConvexityGuarantees any local minimum is the global minimum
Monotonicity\(\lvert y-\hat y_1\rvert < \lvert y-\hat y_2\rvert \Rightarrow L(y,\hat y_1) < L(y,\hat y_2)\)
DifferentiabilityLets us optimise with gradient methods

L1 versus L2

$$L_1(w)=\sum_{i=1}^{n}\bigl\lvert y_i-\hat y_i\bigr\rvert \qquad\qquad L_2(w)=\sum_{i=1}^{n}\bigl(y_i-\hat y_i\bigr)^{2}$$
PropertyL1L2
Non-negativity✓✓
Zero loss for perfect prediction✓✓
Symmetry✓✓
Convexity✓✓
Monotonicity✓✓
Differentiability✗✓

The single row where they differ decides it. L1 is not differentiable at zero, so gradient methods stumble exactly where we want them to land. L2 is smooth everywhere, and it is the only one of the two with a closed-form solution.

Worth knowing

L1's insensitivity to large errors makes it more robust to outliers — squaring gives one bad point enormous influence. That robustness is why L1 still gets used, despite the differentiability problem.

The ordinary least squares objective

Summing squared errors over all points and writing it as a norm:

$$\min_{w}\;\sum_{i=1}^{n}\bigl(y_i-\hat y_i\bigr)^{2} \;=\;\min_{w}\;\lVert y-Xw\rVert^{2}$$
3

Contours: the shape of the error surface

Before doing any algebra, get a feel for the bowl we are about to find the bottom of. Its shape controls everything that follows.

A contour (or level set) joins all points where the function takes the same value — a horizontal slice through the surface, seen from above. For quadratics in two variables the slices are ellipses, and the way they stretch and tilt tells you a great deal.

Six functions, all bowls, all with their minimum at the origin. Only the coefficients change.

1. \(x^2+y^2\)

Equal coefficients, no cross term. The contours are circles — the function grows at the same rate in every direction.

2. \(3x^2+y^2\)

Ellipse elongated along the \(y\)-axis. The \(x\) coefficient is larger, so the function climbs faster in \(x\); to stay on the same level you can travel further in \(y\).

3. \(x^2+3y^2\)

Ellipse elongated along the \(x\)-axis. The mirror image of case 2.

4. \(x^2+y^2-1.4xy\)

Tilted, elongated along \(x=y\). The cross term breaks axis alignment. Because the \(x^2\) and \(y^2\) coefficients are equal, the tilt lands exactly on the 45° diagonal.

5. \(2(x^2+y^2)-1.4xy\)

Still along \(x=y\), but rounder than case 4. Careful here: what changed is the ratio of the cross term to the diagonal terms, not the absolute size of anything. Going from case 4 to case 5 doubled the diagonal coefficients while leaving the cross term at \(-1.4\), so the cross term matters relatively less and the ellipse becomes less eccentric.

Shape versus size

If you scale every coefficient — say \(2x^2+2y^2-2.8xy\) — the shape is identical to case 4 and only the size changes. Shape depends on relative coefficients; size depends on absolute ones.

6. \(0.25x^2+y^2-0.6xy\)

Tilted, but neither along an axis nor along \(x=y\). The elongation sits at roughly 19° from the \(x\)-axis. Unequal diagonal coefficients plus a cross term gives an arbitrary tilt.

The rules

Write any of these as a matrix product. For \(f = ax^2 + 2bxy + cy^2\):

$$f(x,y)=\begin{bmatrix}x & y\end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix}a & b\\ b & c\end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix}x\\ y\end{bmatrix}$$
Mind the 2

The cross term in the matrix is \(b\), but it appears in the function as \(2bxy\). So for \(-1.4xy\), the matrix entry is \(b=-0.7\), not \(-1.4\). This trips up almost everyone the first time.

Case\(a\)\(b\)\(c\)\(ac-b^2\)Contours
\(x^2+y^2\)1011Circle
\(3x^2+y^2\)3013Axis-aligned ellipse, long in \(y\)
\(x^2+3y^2\)1033Axis-aligned ellipse, long in \(x\)
\(x^2+y^2-1.4xy\)1−0.710.51Tilted 45°, elongated
\(2(x^2+y^2)-1.4xy\)2−0.723.51Tilted 45°, rounder
\(0.25x^2+y^2-0.6xy\)0.25−0.310.16Tilted ≈19°

Reading a quadratic without plotting it

  • No cross term \((b=0)\) ⟺ contours are axis-aligned. This works in both directions.
  • Cross term present, \(a=c\) — elongated along \(x=y\) if \(b<0\), along \(x=-y\) if \(b>0\).
  • Cross term present, \(a\ne c\) — tilted at some other angle, given by \(\tan 2\theta = \dfrac{2b}{a-c}\).

But the cross term can also be too large, and then you do not have a bowl at all:

$$ac-b^2 > 0,\ a>0 \;\Rightarrow\; \text{ellipse (a genuine bowl)}$$ $$ac-b^2 < 0 \;\Rightarrow\; \text{hyperbola (a saddle — no minimum)}$$ $$ac-b^2 = 0 \;\Rightarrow\; \text{degenerate — a trough with a flat floor}$$

Try \(x^2+y^2-3xy\): here \(b=-1.5\) and \(ac-b^2 = 1-2.25 < 0\). The contours are hyperbolas and there is no minimum to find. All six cases above pass the test, but the test is not automatic.

Interactive versions of all six surfaces: geogebra.org/m/uehtmkah

Are the contours of \(4x^2 + y^2 - 5xy\) ellipses?

No. Here \(a=4\), \(b=-2.5\), \(c=1\), so \(ac-b^2 = 4 - 6.25 = -2.25 < 0\). The contours are hyperbolas and the function is a saddle with no minimum. The presence of a cross term alone never guarantees an ellipse.

4

Minimising the error, step by step

Expand the objective, differentiate with respect to a vector, set to zero. Nothing here is harder than partial derivatives you already know — it is bookkeeping in matrix clothing.

SymbolShapeMeaning
\(X\)\(n\times d\)Input matrix
\(y\)\(n\times 1\)Observed targets
\(\hat y\)\(n\times 1\)Predicted values, \(\hat y = Xw\)
\(w\)\(d\times 1\)Weight vector

Step 1 — expand the objective

$$\begin{aligned} f(w) &= (y-Xw)^{\top}(y-Xw)\\[4pt] &= y^{\top}y - y^{\top}Xw - (Xw)^{\top}y + (Xw)^{\top}(Xw)\\[4pt] &= y^{\top}y - y^{\top}Xw - w^{\top}X^{\top}y + w^{\top}X^{\top}Xw \end{aligned}$$

Step 2 — the two middle terms are the same number

Check the shapes of \(y^{\top}Xw\):

$$\underbrace{y^{\top}}_{1\times n}\underbrace{X}_{n\times d}\underbrace{w}_{d\times 1}\;=\;\underbrace{c}_{1\times 1}\;=\;\underbrace{w^{\top}}_{1\times d}\underbrace{X^{\top}}_{d\times n}\underbrace{y}_{n\times 1}$$

It is a \(1\times 1\) matrix — a plain number. And every number equals its own transpose, so applying \((ABC)^{\top}=C^{\top}B^{\top}A^{\top}\):

$$y^{\top}Xw = \bigl(y^{\top}Xw\bigr)^{\top} = w^{\top}X^{\top}\bigl(y^{\top}\bigr)^{\top} = w^{\top}X^{\top}y$$

If the transpose gymnastics feel slippery, set \(a = Xw\) and use the fact that the dot product is symmetric:

$$y^{\top}Xw = y^{\top}a = a^{\top}y = (Xw)^{\top}y = w^{\top}X^{\top}y$$

Either way, the two terms collapse into one and the objective becomes

$$f(w)= y^{\top}y \;-\; 2\,y^{\top}Xw \;+\; w^{\top}X^{\top}Xw$$

Three terms: a constant, something linear in \(w\), and something quadratic in \(w\). We differentiate each in turn.

Step 3 — what "differentiate with respect to a vector" means

No new calculus. The gradient is just the ordinary partial derivatives, stacked into a column that has the same shape as \(w\):

$$\nabla_w f = \begin{bmatrix} \partial f/\partial w_1\\[2pt] \partial f/\partial w_2\\[2pt] \vdots\\[2pt] \partial f/\partial w_d \end{bmatrix}_{d\times 1}$$

So the whole job is: differentiate with respect to one weight at a time, then recognise the stack as a matrix product.

Step 4 — the linear term \(-2y^{\top}Xw\)

With \(n=d=3\), first write out \(\hat y = Xw\):

$$\begin{bmatrix} x_{1,1}&x_{1,2}&x_{1,3}\\ x_{2,1}&x_{2,2}&x_{2,3}\\ x_{3,1}&x_{3,2}&x_{3,3} \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix}w_1\\w_2\\w_3\end{bmatrix} =\begin{bmatrix} x_{1,1}w_1+x_{1,2}w_2+x_{1,3}w_3\\ x_{2,1}w_1+x_{2,2}w_2+x_{2,3}w_3\\ x_{3,1}w_1+x_{3,2}w_2+x_{3,3}w_3 \end{bmatrix}$$

Then \(-2y^{\top}Xw = -2\bigl(y_1\hat y_1+y_2\hat y_2+y_3\hat y_3\bigr)\), which written out in full is

$$\begin{aligned} &-2y_1\bigl(x_{1,1}w_1+x_{1,2}w_2+x_{1,3}w_3\bigr)\\ +\;&-2y_2\bigl(x_{2,1}w_1+x_{2,2}w_2+x_{2,3}w_3\bigr)\\ +\;&-2y_3\bigl(x_{3,1}w_1+x_{3,2}w_2+x_{3,3}w_3\bigr) \end{aligned}$$

Now differentiate with respect to \(w_2\). Every term without a \(w_2\) in it is a constant and vanishes; each surviving term drops its \(w_2\):

$$\frac{\partial}{\partial w_2}\Bigl(-2y^{\top}Xw\Bigr) = -2y_1x_{1,2}-2y_2x_{2,2}-2y_3x_{3,2} = -2\sum_{i=1}^{n} y_i x_{i,2}$$

Compare that with the second entry of \(X^{\top}y\):

$$\begin{bmatrix} x_{1,1}&x_{2,1}&x_{3,1}\\ x_{1,2}&x_{2,2}&x_{3,2}\\ x_{1,3}&x_{2,3}&x_{3,3} \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix}y_1\\y_2\\y_3\end{bmatrix} =\begin{bmatrix} x_{1,1}y_1+x_{2,1}y_2+x_{3,1}y_3\\ \boxed{x_{1,2}y_1+x_{2,2}y_2+x_{3,2}y_3}\\ x_{1,3}y_1+x_{2,3}y_2+x_{3,3}y_3 \end{bmatrix} =\begin{bmatrix}(X^{\top}y)_1\\ (X^{\top}y)_2\\ (X^{\top}y)_3\end{bmatrix}$$

They match exactly. In general, for any \(w_k\):

$$\frac{\partial}{\partial w_k}\Bigl(-2y^{\top}Xw\Bigr) = -2\,\bigl(X^{\top}y\bigr)_k = -2\sum_{i=1}^{n}y_i x_{ik}$$

Stack over all \(k\):

$$\nabla_w\bigl(-2y^{\top}Xw\bigr) = -2X^{\top}y$$
Why \(X^{\top}y\) and not \(y^{\top}X\)?

They are the same \(d\) numbers — one is a row, one is a column, and they are transposes of each other. We pick \(X^{\top}y\) because the gradient must have the same shape as \(w\), i.e. \(d\times 1\), and \(X^{\top}y\) is already a column. Choosing \(y^{\top}X\) is not wrong; it just forces you to transpose at the very last step instead.

Step 5 — the quadratic term \(w^{\top}X^{\top}Xw\)

Name the inner product to keep the algebra readable:

$$A_{d\times d}=X^{\top}_{d\times n}X_{n\times d}\qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad w^{\top}X^{\top}Xw = w^{\top}Aw$$

Written out for \(n=d=3\), the entries of \(A\) are sums of products of feature columns:

$$A=\begin{bmatrix} \textstyle\sum_i x_{i,1}^{2} & \textstyle\sum_i x_{i,1}x_{i,2} & \textstyle\sum_i x_{i,1}x_{i,3}\\[3pt] \textstyle\sum_i x_{i,1}x_{i,2} & \textstyle\sum_i x_{i,2}^{2} & \textstyle\sum_i x_{i,2}x_{i,3}\\[3pt] \textstyle\sum_i x_{i,1}x_{i,3} & \textstyle\sum_i x_{i,2}x_{i,3} & \textstyle\sum_i x_{i,3}^{2} \end{bmatrix}$$

Every off-diagonal entry appears twice, mirrored across the diagonal. \(A\) is symmetric, and that fact does real work in a moment.

Expanding \(w^{\top}Aw\):

$$w^{\top}Aw=\sum_{i=1}^{d}\sum_{j=1}^{d}A_{ij}\,w_i w_j$$

Differentiate with respect to one weight \(w_k\) and sort the terms into four groups:

GroupTermsDerivative w.r.t. \(w_k\)
\(i=j=k\)\(A_{kk}w_k^2\)\(2A_{kk}w_k\)
\(i=k,\ j\ne k\)\(A_{kj}w_kw_j\)\(\sum_{j\ne k}A_{kj}w_j\)
\(j=k,\ i\ne k\)\(A_{ik}w_iw_k\)\(\sum_{i\ne k}A_{ik}w_i\)
neither\(A_{ij}w_iw_j\)0 — constant

Because \(A\) is symmetric, \(A_{ik}=A_{ki}\), so groups two and three are equal. Everything collects into

$$\frac{\partial}{\partial w_k}\bigl(w^{\top}Aw\bigr)=2\sum_{j=1}^{d}A_{kj}w_j = 2\,(Aw)_k$$

The \(k\)-th partial derivative is exactly twice the \(k\)-th entry of \(Aw\). Stacking over \(k\):

$$\nabla_w\bigl(w^{\top}Aw\bigr)=\bigl(A+A^{\top}\bigr)w \;\overset{A=A^{\top}}{=}\; 2Aw \;=\; 2X^{\top}Xw$$
Symmetry is doing work here

The general rule is \(\nabla_w(w^{\top}Aw)=(A+A^{\top})w\). It collapses to \(2Aw\) only because \(A=X^{\top}X\) is symmetric. That is not decoration — for a non-symmetric \(A\) the answer would be different.

The same result on a small case

With \(d=2\) and \(A\) symmetric, \(w^{\top}Aw = A_{11}w_1^2 + 2A_{12}w_1w_2 + A_{22}w_2^2\), so

$$\frac{\partial}{\partial w_1}=2A_{11}w_1+2A_{12}w_2,\qquad \frac{\partial}{\partial w_2}=2A_{12}w_1+2A_{22}w_2$$

Stack them, factor out the 2, and the result is visibly \(2Aw\).

Step 6 — set the gradient to zero

$$\nabla_w f(w) = -2X^{\top}y + 2X^{\top}Xw = 0$$

Rearranging gives the normal equations:

$$X^{\top}Xw = X^{\top}y$$

And solving for \(w\):

$$w=\bigl(X^{\top}X\bigr)^{-1}X^{\top}y$$
Small worked example

Fit \(y = wx\) (no intercept) to \(\{(-1,1),(2,-5),(3,5)\}\). Here \(X=[-1,2,3]^{\top}\), \(y=[1,-5,5]^{\top}\), so \(X^{\top}X = 1+4+9 = 14\) and \(X^{\top}y = -1-10+15 = 4\). Therefore \(w = 4/14 \approx 0.286\).

With \(d=1\), \(X^{\top}X\) is just a number, so the whole formula collapses to \(w=\dfrac{\sum_i x_iy_i}{\sum_i x_i^2}\) — the familiar no-intercept slope.

In that example, do the residuals sum to zero?

No. The fitted values are \(\hat y = \bigl[-\tfrac{2}{7},\tfrac{4}{7},\tfrac{6}{7}\bigr]\), giving residuals \(\bigl[\tfrac{9}{7},-\tfrac{39}{7},\tfrac{29}{7}\bigr]\), which sum to \(-\tfrac{1}{7}\). Residuals summing to zero requires an intercept column of ones, and this model has none. What does still hold is \(X^{\top}r = \tfrac{1}{7}(-9-78+87) = 0\) — orthogonality to the feature that is present.

5

What the closed form costs

We have an exact answer. So why is there a Lecture 3 at all?

Breaking the formula \(w=(X^{\top}X)^{-1}X^{\top}y\) into its two expensive pieces:

StepCost
Form \(X^{\top}X\) (an \(n\times d\) times \(d\times n\) product)\(O(nd^2)\)
Solve the \(d\times d\) system\(O(d^3)\)
$$\text{Total: } O\!\left(nd^{2}+d^{3}\right)$$

Linear in \(n\), cubic in \(d\). That asymmetry is the whole story. A million rows is fine. Fifty thousand features is not — the matrix inversion alone dominates everything else, and it does not care how much data you have.

So when \(d\) is large, we need a method that never forms or inverts a \(d\times d\) matrix. That method is gradient descent.

6

Least squares is a projection

The closed form is not an algebraic accident. It is the answer to a question about perpendicular distance.

The picture in three dimensions

Take three observations and two features — age and salary, say. The design matrix \(X\in\mathbb{R}^{3\times 2}\) is most useful here read column by column:

$$X=\begin{bmatrix} \big| & \big| \\[2pt] \mathbf{d}_1 & \mathbf{d}_2 \\[2pt] \big| & \big| \end{bmatrix}, \qquad \mathbf{d}_1,\mathbf{d}_2\in\mathbb{R}^{3},\qquad \mathbf{y}\in\mathbb{R}^{3}$$

Each column is one feature recorded across all three observations, so it lives in \(\mathbb{R}^{3}\). The labels live there too. The three axes of that space are not features — each axis is one data point.

Every prediction the model can make has the form \(X\boldsymbol\alpha\), and

$$X\boldsymbol\alpha=\alpha_1\mathbf{d}_1+\alpha_2\mathbf{d}_2$$

So the reachable predictions are every linear combination of two vectors in \(\mathbb{R}^{3}\): a plane through the origin, the column space \(\mathcal{C}(X)\). Two knobs, three dimensions to fill.

Why \(\mathbf{y}\) misses the plane

The plane is two-dimensional and sits inside a three-dimensional space, so a vector chosen without reference to it will not lie in it. This is the general situation whenever \(n>d\): more equations than unknowns, so \(X\boldsymbol\alpha=\mathbf{y}\) has no exact solution and the residual cannot be driven to zero.

Since we cannot reach \(\mathbf{y}\), we settle for the point of the plane that comes closest to it:

$$\min_{\boldsymbol\alpha\in\mathbb{R}^{2}}\ \bigl\lVert \mathbf{y}-X\boldsymbol\alpha \bigr\rVert_2^{2}$$

which is exactly the least-squares objective. Read this way, the sum of squared errors is not an arbitrary scoring rule — it is squared Euclidean distance in \(\mathbb{R}^{n}\), and minimising it means finding a nearest point.

The condition that finds the closest point

Drop a perpendicular from \(\mathbf{y}\) to the plane. The foot of that perpendicular is the closest point, and its defining property is that the segment joining it to \(\mathbf{y}\) meets the plane at a right angle. Writing \(\mathbf{r}=\mathbf{y}-X\boldsymbol\alpha\), the residual must be orthogonal to every vector in the plane — and it is enough to check the two spanning vectors, since everything else is a combination of them:

$$\mathbf{d}_1^{\top}\mathbf{r}=0 \quad\text{and}\quad \mathbf{d}_2^{\top}\mathbf{r}=0$$

Those two scalar equations stack into one matrix equation, because the rows of \(X^{\top}\) are precisely \(\mathbf{d}_1^{\top}\) and \(\mathbf{d}_2^{\top}\):

$$X^{\top}\bigl(\mathbf{y}-X\boldsymbol\alpha\bigr)=\mathbf{0}$$

Solving it

Expand and collect the terms in \(\boldsymbol\alpha\):

$$X^{\top}\mathbf{y}-X^{\top}X\boldsymbol\alpha=\mathbf{0} \qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad X^{\top}X\boldsymbol\alpha=X^{\top}\mathbf{y}$$

These are the normal equations. When \(\mathbf{d}_1\) and \(\mathbf{d}_2\) are linearly independent — that is, when the plane is genuinely two-dimensional rather than collapsed to a line — the matrix \(X^{\top}X\) is invertible and

$$\boldsymbol\alpha=(X^{\top}X)^{-1}X^{\top}\mathbf{y}\;=\;\mathbf{w}^{\star}$$

The closed-form solution was never anything other than the coordinates of the foot of the perpendicular. The two entries of \(\mathbf{w}^{\star}\) say how much \(\mathbf{d}_1\) and how much \(\mathbf{d}_2\) to mix in order to land on the closest point.

Checking the substitution

Run the argument backwards to confirm \(\mathbf{w}^{\star}\) really does make the residual perpendicular:

$$X^{\top}\bigl(\mathbf{y}-X\mathbf{w}^{\star}\bigr) = X^{\top}\mathbf{y}-\underbrace{X^{\top}X\,(X^{\top}X)^{-1}}_{=\ I}X^{\top}\mathbf{y} = X^{\top}\mathbf{y}-X^{\top}\mathbf{y}=\mathbf{0}$$

The whole cancellation rests on nothing more than the definition of the inverse. The residual is orthogonal to both feature columns, so \(X\mathbf{w}^{\star}\) is the foot of the perpendicular and no other point of the plane is nearer to \(\mathbf{y}\).

The scalar form

The condition is often written against the fitted vector itself. It follows in one line from the result above:

$$\bigl(\mathbf{y}-X\mathbf{w}^{\star}\bigr)^{\top}\bigl(X\mathbf{w}^{\star}\bigr) =(\mathbf{w}^{\star})^{\top}\underbrace{X^{\top}\bigl(\mathbf{y}-X\mathbf{w}^{\star}\bigr)}_{=\ \mathbf{0}}=0$$
Why it must be every vector, not just one

The scalar form says the residual is perpendicular to one particular vector, \(X\boldsymbol\alpha\). The matrix form says it is perpendicular to every vector in the plane. The second implies the first, but not the reverse — on its own, the scalar condition places the foot anywhere on a sphere having \(\mathbf{0}\) and \(\mathbf{y}\) as opposite poles, which meets the plane in a whole circle rather than at a point.

So the scalar identity is a useful consistency check, while \(X^{\top}(\mathbf{y}-X\boldsymbol\alpha)=\mathbf{0}\) is the condition that actually pins down the answer.

What the picture buys you

Write the fitted vector out in full:

$$\hat{\mathbf{y}}=X\mathbf{w}^{\star}=\underbrace{X(X^{\top}X)^{-1}X^{\top}}_{\textstyle H}\,\mathbf{y}$$

Fitting is a linear map applied to the labels, and \(H\) — the hat matrix — is what performs the projection. Its two defining properties read straight off the figure. It is symmetric, and it satisfies \(H^{2}=H\): once \(\mathbf{y}\) has been flattened onto the plane it is already there, so flattening it again does nothing.

The right angle also gives Pythagoras, since \(\mathbf{y}=\hat{\mathbf{y}}+\mathbf{r}\) with \(\hat{\mathbf{y}}\perp\mathbf{r}\):

$$\lVert\mathbf{y}\rVert^{2}=\lVert\hat{\mathbf{y}}\rVert^{2}+\lVert\mathbf{y}-\hat{\mathbf{y}}\rVert^{2}$$
Three things that fall out of one right angle

That last identity is the variance decomposition behind \(R^{2}\). Orthogonality against the intercept column reads \(\sum_i r_i=0\), so the residuals of a model with an intercept must sum to zero — and vanish that column and the guarantee goes with it.

And if \(\mathbf{d}_1\) and \(\mathbf{d}_2\) are nearly parallel, the plane is still two-dimensional but only barely. The foot of the perpendicular stays well defined — \(\hat{\mathbf{y}}\) is unique regardless — but the coordinates \(\mathbf{w}^{\star}\) describing how to reach it become wildly unstable. That is multicollinearity, seen geometrically.

7

Gradient descent

Instead of jumping to the bottom of the bowl in one calculation, walk downhill in small steps.

Two facts that make it work

  1. Mean squared error is convex. So if we keep going downhill at a reasonably small pace, we are guaranteed to reach the global minimum. There are no local minima to get stuck in.
  2. The gradient points in the direction of steepest ascent. So moving in the opposite direction takes us closer to the minimum.
$$w^{(k+1)} = w^{(k)} - \alpha\,\nabla_w J$$

\(\alpha\) is the learning rate — how far we move along that direction each step.

Working it out on a simple model

Take the loss function and a one-feature model:

$$J(w)=\frac{1}{2n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\Bigl(y^{(i)}-\hat y^{(i)}\Bigr)^{2}, \qquad \hat y^{(i)} = w_0 + w_1x^{(i)}$$

Substituting the model into the loss:

$$J(w)=\frac{1}{2n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\Bigl(y^{(i)}-w_0-w_1x^{(i)}\Bigr)^{2}$$
Where the \(\tfrac{1}{2n}\) comes from

The \(\tfrac{1}{n}\) makes the loss an average rather than a sum, so it does not grow with dataset size. The \(\tfrac{1}{2}\) is pure convenience: differentiating a square brings down a 2 that cancels it, leaving clean formulas. Neither changes where the minimum is — only the scale of the loss, and hence the useful range of \(\alpha\).

Each weight gets its own update, using its own partial derivative:

$$w_0^{(k+1)}=w_0^{(k)}-\alpha\frac{\partial J}{\partial w_0}, \qquad w_1^{(k+1)}=w_1^{(k)}-\alpha\frac{\partial J}{\partial w_1}$$

Derivative with respect to \(w_0\)

Apply the chain rule. The inner derivative of \(\bigl(y^{(i)}-w_0-w_1x^{(i)}\bigr)\) with respect to \(w_0\) is \(-1\):

$$\frac{\partial J}{\partial w_0}=\frac{1}{2n}\times 2\sum_{i=1}^{n}\Bigl(y^{(i)}-w_0-w_1x^{(i)}\Bigr)\times(-1)$$ $$\frac{\partial J}{\partial w_0}=\frac{-1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\Bigl(y^{(i)}-\hat y^{(i)}\Bigr)$$

Derivative with respect to \(w_1\)

Same chain rule, but now the inner derivative is \(-x^{(i)}\):

$$\frac{\partial J}{\partial w_1}=\frac{-1}{2n}\times 2\sum_{i=1}^{n}\Bigl(y^{(i)}-w_0-w_1x^{(i)}\Bigr)\times\frac{\partial}{\partial w_1}\Bigl(w_1x^{(i)}\Bigr)$$ $$\frac{\partial J}{\partial w_1}=\frac{-1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\Bigl(y^{(i)}-\hat y^{(i)}\Bigr)\times x^{(i)}$$

The general model

For \(\hat y^{(i)} = w_0x_0^{(i)} + w_1x_1^{(i)} + w_2x_2^{(i)} + \dots + w_kx_k^{(i)}\) (with \(x_0 \equiv 1\)):

$$\frac{\partial J}{\partial w_p}=\frac{-1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\Bigl(y^{(i)}-\hat y^{(i)}\Bigr)\times x_p^{(i)}$$

One formula covers every weight. Notice \(w_0\) is just the case \(p=0\), where \(x_0=1\) — which is why the augmented form from block 1 was worth setting up.

Read the formula

The gradient for weight \(p\) is the error, weighted by the feature it belongs to. A feature that is large when the error is large gets a large gradient. Hold on to that sentence — it is the entire explanation for why feature scaling matters in block 9.

8

The procedure and when to stop

The full algorithm, and the practical question of how you know you have arrived.

Stopping criteria

Ideally we would stop when the gradient is exactly zero:

$$\nabla_w J(w)=0$$

But that is not always reachable — it might take infinite iterations. So decide on some precision, say \(\varepsilon \approx 10^{-5}\), and use one of these instead.

CriterionTestCaution
Gradient magnitude \(\lVert\nabla_w J(w^{(k)})\rVert \le \varepsilon\) The most direct statement of "we have arrived"
Change in parameters \(\lVert w^{(k+1)}-w^{(k)}\rVert \le \varepsilon\) Can give a false positive if the learning rate is too small — tiny steps look like convergence even when you are far from the minimum
Change in cost \(\lvert J(w^{(k+1)})-J(w^{(k)})\rvert \le \varepsilon\) Same trap, plus a flat plateau can stall it

In practice you also cap the number of iterations, so a diverging run terminates instead of overflowing.

The general procedure

  1. Decide on \(\alpha\), \(\varepsilon\), and the stopping criterion.
  2. Make an initial guess \(w = w^{(0)}\).
  3. Calculate updated weights: \(w^{(k+1)} = w^{(k)} - \alpha\nabla_w J\).
  4. Check the stopping criterion. If satisfied, stop. If not, go back to step 3.

The same procedure for linear regression

Substituting the gradient we derived in block 7, step 3 becomes concrete:

$$w^{(k+1)} = w^{(k)} - \frac{\alpha}{n}\sum_{i}\Bigl(\hat{y}^{(i)} - y^{(i)}\Bigr)x^{(i)}$$
Mind the sign

The gradient \(\dfrac{\partial J}{\partial w_p}=\dfrac{-1}{n}\sum_i(y^{(i)}-\hat y^{(i)})x_p^{(i)}\) already carries a minus sign. The update rule subtracts the gradient, so the two minuses cancel and the sum is added. Writing \(w^{(k)}-\frac{\alpha}{n}\sum_i(y^{(i)}-\hat y^{(i)})x^{(i)}\) double-negates and sends you uphill. Alternatively, you can write it as: $$w^{(k+1)} = w^{(k)} + \frac{\alpha}{n}\sum_{i}\Bigl(y^{(i)} - \hat{y}^{(i)}\Bigr)x^{(i)}$$

Your loss decreases for 50 iterations, then stays flat at a value well above zero. Have you converged?

Not necessarily. A flat loss curve satisfies the "change in cost" criterion, but it can also mean the learning rate is too small to make visible progress, or that you are oscillating across a narrow valley (block 8, the oscillation case, has a loss curve that flattens at 45 while \(w_1\) bounces forever). Check the gradient magnitude and the parameter trajectory before declaring victory.

9

Choosing the learning rate

One number decides whether gradient descent crawls, converges, bounces forever, or explodes. Here is how to predict which, without running anything.

The test function

$$J(w)=5w_1^{2}+w_2^{2}$$

Each coordinate is just multiplied by a number

Start in one variable, \(J(w)=5w^2\). Then \(\dfrac{dJ}{dw}=10w\), and the update is

$$w^{\text{new}} = w - \alpha(10w) = (1-10\alpha)\,w$$

That is the whole idea. Each step multiplies \(w\) by a fixed number. Call it the multiplier \(r = 1-10\alpha\). After \(k\) steps, \(w^{(k)} = r^k w^{(0)}\).

Multiplier \(r\)What happens
\(0 < r < 1\)Shrinks toward 0, keeping its sign — smooth decay
\(r = 0\)Jumps to 0 in a single step
\(-1 < r < 0\)Shrinks toward 0, but flips sign every step
\(r = -1\)Flips forever without shrinking
\(r < -1\)Flips and grows — diverges

So convergence needs \(\lvert r\rvert < 1\):

$$\lvert 1-10\alpha\rvert < 1 \;\Longrightarrow\; -1 < 1-10\alpha < 1 \;\Longrightarrow\; 0 < \alpha < 0.2$$

Two variables that do not interact

Back to \(J(w_1,w_2)=5w_1^2+w_2^2\). The partial derivatives are

$$\frac{\partial J}{\partial w_1}=10w_1,\qquad \frac{\partial J}{\partial w_2}=2w_2$$

Neither contains the other variable, so the two coordinates update completely independently — two separate one-dimensional problems running side by side, each with its own multiplier:

$$w_1^{\text{new}}=(1-10\alpha)\,w_1,\qquad w_2^{\text{new}}=(1-2\alpha)\,w_2$$

One learning rate, two different multipliers, because the coefficients 5 and 1 differ. Everything below follows from those two numbers.

Case\(\alpha\)\(r_1 = 1-10\alpha\)\(r_2 = 1-2\alpha\)Behaviour
Slow0.030.700.94Both converge; \(w_2\) shrinks only 6% per step
Rapid0.100.000.80\(w_1\) dies in one step; \(w_2\) decays 20% per step
Oscillation0.20−1.000.60\(w_1\) flips \(3,-3,3,\dots\) forever
Divergence0.25−1.500.50\(\lvert r_1\rvert > 1\), so \(w_1\) explodes

Now \(\lvert r_1\rvert = 1.5 > 1\), so \(w_1\) grows by 50% and flips sign every step. Within 30 iterations the loss reaches \(1.65\times10^{12}\).

Divergence is partial

Look again at the parameter plot: \(w_2\) converges beautifully, because \(r_2 = 0.5\). Only \(w_1\) blows up. One bad direction ruins everything — which is exactly why the safe learning rate is dictated by the steepest direction, not the average one.

Diagnosing from the loss curve

What you seeWhat it meansFix
Smooth decrease to a low value\(\alpha\) is in a good rangeNothing
Decreasing, but barely\(\alpha\) too smallIncrease \(\alpha\), often by 3× at a time
Drops then flattens highOscillating in the steep directionReduce \(\alpha\)
Sawtooth or increasing\(\alpha\) above the stability thresholdReduce \(\alpha\) sharply; check feature scaling
For \(J = 8w_1^2 + 2w_2^2\), what is the largest \(\alpha\) that converges, and what \(\alpha\) kills \(w_1\) in one step?

The multipliers are \(1-16\alpha\) and \(1-4\alpha\). Convergence needs \(\lvert 1-16\alpha\rvert<1\), so \(\alpha < 1/8 = 0.125\). Setting \(1-16\alpha=0\) gives \(\alpha = 1/16 = 0.0625\), which zeroes \(w_1\) immediately and leaves \(w_2\) with multiplier \(0.75\).

10

Feature scaling

What goes wrong when one feature is measured in thousands and another in tenths — and why no single learning rate can fix it.

A two-point example that breaks

$$\hat y = w_0+w_1x_1+w_2x_2,\qquad J(w)=\frac{1}{2n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\Bigl(y^{(i)}-w_0-w_1x_1^{(i)}-w_2x_2^{(i)}\Bigr)^2$$
\(x_1\)\(x_2\)\(y\)
\(x^{(1)}\)0.11005
\(x^{(2)}\)0.550025

Feature 2 is a thousand times larger than feature 1. Initialise everything at zero: \(w_0=w_1=w_2=0\), so \(\hat y^{(1)} = \hat y^{(2)} = 0\) and the errors are the full targets, 5 and 25.

Now compute the three gradients using \(\dfrac{\partial J}{\partial w_p}=\dfrac{-1}{n}\sum_i\bigl(y^{(i)}-\hat y^{(i)}\bigr)x_p^{(i)}\):

$$\begin{aligned} \frac{\partial J}{\partial w_0}&=\frac{-1}{2}\bigl((5-0)\times 1+(25-0)\times 1\bigr)&&=\;-15\\[6pt] \frac{\partial J}{\partial w_1}&=\frac{-1}{2}\bigl((5-0)\times 0.1+(25-0)\times 0.5\bigr)&&=\;-6.5\\[6pt] \frac{\partial J}{\partial w_2}&=\frac{-1}{2}\bigl((5-0)\times 100+(25-0)\times 500\bigr)&&=\;-6500 \end{aligned}$$

The third gradient is a thousand times the second — not because feature 2 is more useful, but purely because its numbers are bigger.

What happens next

With \(\alpha = 0.001\), the weights do not converge — they detonate.

Iteration\(w_0\)\(w_1\)\(w_2\)
1000
20.0150.00656.5
3−1.92001695−0.832−832
4247.698756168107.335107335.87
5−31953.3282445837−13846.40946−13846409.466

Since \(x_2 \gg x_1\), the gradient with respect to \(w_2\) is far larger, causing huge jumps in the weights. A learning rate small enough to keep \(w_2\) stable would leave \(w_1\) frozen; a rate large enough to move \(w_1\) sends \(w_2\) to infinity. No single \(\alpha\) works for both.

Weights and importance

  • Weights in some sense measure the importance of a feature.
  • But because \(x_2 \gg x_1\), we get \(\dfrac{\partial J}{\partial w_2} \gg \dfrac{\partial J}{\partial w_1}\), and therefore \(w_2 \gg w_1\).
  • We cannot conclude from this that \(w_2\) is more important than \(w_1\) for the underlying data.
  • If a feature has a large value, its corresponding weight may grow very large even if it is not more important.
  • So observing a large weight does not necessarily indicate greater feature importance.

What scaling fixes

Feature scaling — standardization or normalization — puts all features on a similar scale, so that:

  • gradients are comparable across weights;
  • weight magnitudes more accurately reflect feature contribution;
  • the contours become rounder, so gradient descent converges in far fewer steps.

Without scaling, features with larger numeric values dominate the learning process and mislead interpretation.

Two ways to scale

Min-max scaling

$$x' = \frac{x-x_{\min}}{x_{\max}-x_{\min}},\qquad x'\in[0,1]$$

Worked on two features of very different scale:

$$\begin{aligned} x_1 = [5,\,7,\,11] \;&\longrightarrow\; x_1' = [0,\;0.33,\;1]\\ x_2 = [5000,\,8000,\,15000] \;&\longrightarrow\; x_2' = [0,\;0.3,\;1] \end{aligned}$$

Standardization (z-score)

$$x' = \frac{x-\mu}{\sigma},\qquad \mu=\text{mean},\ \sigma=\text{standard deviation}$$
$$\begin{aligned} x_1 = [5,\,7,\,11],\ \ \mu=7.667,\ \sigma=2.495 \;&\longrightarrow\; x_1' = [-1.07,\;-0.27,\;1.33]\\ x_2 = [5000,\,8000,\,15000],\ \ \mu=9333.3,\ \sigma=4190.5 \;&\longrightarrow\; x_2' = [-1.034,\;-0.318,\;1.35] \end{aligned}$$

Both put the two features on comparable footing. Min-max forces a fixed range but is sensitive to outliers, since a single extreme value sets an endpoint. Standardization is unbounded but far more robust, and it is the usual default.

Fit on train only

Compute \(x_{\min}, x_{\max}, \mu, \sigma\) on the training set alone, then apply those same numbers to validation and test data. Computing them over the full dataset leaks information about the test set into training and gives optimistic results.

Does the closed-form solution need feature scaling too?

Not for accuracy. Replacing \(X\) with \(XM\) for any invertible \(M\) gives the new solution \(M^{-1}w\), and \((XM)(M^{-1}w) = Xw\) — the predictions are identical. So plain OLS is invariant to rescaling; only the coefficient values relabel. Scaling still helps numerically (conditioning) and for interpretation. But this invariance disappears under ridge and lasso, because the penalty \(\lambda\lVert w\rVert^2\) depends on the parametrisation — which is why you must standardize before regularizing.

11

Batch, stochastic, mini-batch

Three variants of the same algorithm. They differ in one thing only: how many data points you look at before taking a step.

All three minimise the same average loss

$$J(w)=\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}J_i(w)$$

and differ only in how many terms are summed before updating \(w\).

Batch gradient descent

$$w_k := w_k - \alpha\times\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N}\frac{\partial J^{(i)}}{\partial w_k}$$
  • Uses all \(n\) points per update. One pass over the data gives one update.
  • The gradient is exact, so descent is smooth and monotone for a suitable \(\alpha\).
  • On a convex problem it converges to the exact minimum with a fixed \(\alpha\).
  • Requires the whole dataset available for every step.
  • Painful for large \(n\): you compute a million gradients to move once.

Stochastic gradient descent

$$w_k := w_k - \alpha\times\frac{\partial J^{(i)}}{\partial w_k}\qquad i \text{ chosen at random}$$
  • Uses exactly 1 point per update. One pass over the data gives \(n\) updates.
  • The gradient is extremely noisy, so the descent path is erratic and bounces around the minimum.
  • On a convex problem, it requires a decaying \(\alpha\) to converge completely to the exact minimum.
  • Requires minimal memory since it processes only one example at a time.
  • Computationally cheap per step, but fails to utilize hardware vectorization for fast matrix operations.

Mini-batch gradient descent

$$w_k := w_k - \alpha\times\frac{1}{m}\sum_{i=1}^{m}\frac{\partial J^{(i)}}{\partial w_k}$$
  • Uses a small subset of \(m\) points (e.g., 32, 64, or 256) per update. One pass over the data gives \(n/m\) updates.
  • The gradient is mildly noisy, balancing stability with the ability to escape shallow local minima.
  • Converges reliably, but typically requires a decaying \(\alpha\) to settle exactly at the final minimum.
  • Strikes a practical balance by fitting into GPU memory while heavily leveraging fast vectorized operations.
  • Introduces the batch size \(m\) as an additional hyperparameter that you must tune.

Comparison

BatchStochasticMini-batch
Points per update\(n\)1\(m\)
Updates per epoch1\(n\)\(n/m\)
Gradientexactunbiased, high varianceunbiased, variance \(\propto 1/m\)
Pathsmoothvery noisymildly noisy
With fixed \(\alpha\), converges tothe minimuma noise balla smaller noise ball
Memory neededall dataone pointone batch
Vectorises wellyespoorlyyes
A common misconception

SGD is not cheaper per epoch. All three compute \(n\) gradients per pass, so all three cost \(O(nd)\) of gradient work per epoch. Counting the weight updates too, SGD actually does slightly more work, since each of its \(n\) updates costs \(O(d)\).

What differs is how that identical budget is spent. The same \(O(nd)\) buys batch one exact step and SGD \(n\) rough ones. Rough steps are individually worse but not \(n\) times worse — early on, when you are far from the optimum, almost any descent direction helps. So SGD makes much more progress per unit of work, right up until you need high precision, where its noise floor bites and only a decaying step size removes it.

Epoch, iteration, update

An epoch is one full pass through the training set. An iteration or update is one change to \(w\). These are the same thing only for batch gradient descent.

Typical exam question

With \(n = 10{,}000\) samples, batch size 100, trained for 20 epochs — how many weight updates occur?

Updates per epoch \(= 10{,}000/100 = 100\). Over 20 epochs, \(100\times 20 = \mathbf{2000}\) updates.

One practical warning: shuffle the data. If it arrives sorted by label or by any feature, un-shuffled SGD sees systematically biased gradients within each stretch of the pass.

12

Bias and variance

A model can fail by being too simple or by being too eager. These are different failures and they need opposite fixes.

The setup

Data generated from \(\sin x\) with noise added. The green curve is the truth we are trying to recover; in reality we never see it.

Degree 1 — underfitting

Degree 3 — appropriate capacity

Degree 9 — overfitting

This is still linear regression

Fitting \(w_0+w_1x+\dots+w_9x^9\) is ordinary least squares on a transformed design matrix whose columns are \(1, x, x^2,\dots,x^9\). "Linear" means linear in the parameters, not linear in the inputs. Every formula from block 4 applies unchanged.

Capacity against error

The dartboard

QuadrantReadingExample
High bias, low variance
Underfitting		 Darts tightly clustered but far from the centre. The model gives consistent predictions that consistently miss the true target. A linear model on a non-linear problem
Low bias, high variance
Overfitting		 Darts spread out but centred on the bullseye. The model is capable of hitting the target, but its predictions swing wildly with the training data. A complex model that overfits
High bias, high variance Spread out and off-centre. Inaccurate and inconsistent. Poor model choice plus fitting to noise
Low bias, low variance
Ideal		 Tight cluster on the bullseye. Accurate and consistent. A well-tuned model with enough capacity

The definitions

$$\text{Bias} = \mathbb{E}\bigl[\hat Y\bigr] - Y \qquad\qquad \text{Variance} = \mathbb{E}\Bigl\{\bigl[\hat Y-\mathbb{E}[\hat Y]\bigr]^{2}\Bigr\}$$

Bias is the difference between the model's average prediction and the true value. Variance is how much the predictions of the model move when it is retrained on different datasets.

Get the expectation in the right place

Squared bias is \(\bigl(\mathbb{E}[\hat Y]-Y\bigr)^{2}\) — the expectation goes inside the bracket. Writing \(\mathbb{E}\{[\hat Y-Y]^2\}\) gives the mean squared error, not the squared bias, and then bias² + variance double-counts.

The decomposition

$$\mathbb{E}\bigl[(y-\hat f)^{2}\bigr] = \underbrace{\text{Bias}^{2}}_{\text{too simple}} + \underbrace{\text{Variance}}_{\text{too sensitive}} + \underbrace{\sigma^{2}}_{\text{irreducible}}$$

That third term is noise in the data itself. No model, however good, removes it — which is why test error never reaches zero and why a model that appears to beat \(\sigma^2\) on training data is memorising noise.

Diagnosing which problem you have

Split the data — training set (say 70%) to learn the parameters, validation set (15%) to test model quality and determine bias versus variance, and a test set (15%) held back for the final estimate. Then read the two errors together.

Training errorValidation errorInterpretation
HighHighUnderfitting / high bias. The model is too simple to fit even the training data.
HighLowUnusual. Could indicate noise in the training set, a data leak, or a very small training set. Uncommon in practice.
LowHighOverfitting / high variance. Fits the training data very well but fails to generalize.
LowLowGood fit. Low bias and low variance — fits and generalizes.
Training error 2%, validation error 24%. What do you do?

High variance. Collecting more data helps, and so does reducing capacity — fewer features, a lower polynomial degree, or regularization (block 14). Note what would not help: adding features or training longer, both of which increase variance further. Contrast with training 22% / validation 24%, which is high bias, where more data does nothing and you need a richer model instead.

13

Validation

How to estimate performance on data the model has never seen, without burning through your dataset.

Cross-validation checks how well a model performs on unseen data while preventing overfitting. It works by:

  • splitting the dataset into several parts;
  • training the model on some parts and testing it on the remaining part;
  • repeating this resampling process multiple times, choosing different parts each time;
  • averaging the results from each validation step to get the final performance.

Hold-out validation

  • Divide the dataset into non-overlapping training and testing sets.
  • Typical split ratios are 70:30, 80:20 or 60:40, depending on dataset size.
  • The training set fits the model; the test set evaluates performance metrics.

Simple and cheap, but the estimate depends heavily on which points happened to land in the test set — a real problem when data is scarce.

Leave-one-out cross validation (LOOCV)

The model is trained on the entire dataset except for one data point, which is used for testing. This is repeated for each data point in the dataset.

  • All data points are used for training, resulting in low bias.
  • Testing on a single data point can cause high variance, especially if that point is an outlier.
  • Very time-consuming for large datasets, since it requires one full training run per data point.

K-fold cross validation

K-fold splits the dataset into \(k\) equal-sized folds. The model is trained on \(k-1\) folds and tested on the remaining fold, and the process repeats \(k\) times, each time using a different fold for testing.

  1. Decide the number of folds, \(K\).
  2. Randomly divide the dataset into \(K\) equal parts.
  3. Select the first fold as the test set and use the remaining \(K-1\) folds to train.
  4. Test on the selected fold and record the result.
  5. Repeat \(K\) times, each time using a different fold as the test set.
  6. Average all \(K\) results to get the final performance score.
Round 120%20%20%20%20%
Round 220%20%20%20%20%
Round 320%20%20%20%20%
Round 420%20%20%20%20%
Round 520%20%20%20%20%
Validation fold Training folds

Every point is used for validation exactly once and for training \(k-1\) times. LOOCV is the special case \(k=n\). Typical choices are \(k=5\) or \(k=10\), which balance the cost of \(k\) training runs against the stability of the estimate.

With 10-fold cross validation on 1000 samples, how many models are trained and how large is each training set?

Ten models, each trained on 900 samples and validated on the held-out 100. The reported score is the average of the ten validation results. Note this is ten times the cost of a single hold-out split — the price you pay for a more stable estimate.

14

Regularization

If overfitting comes from too much model complexity, penalise complexity directly rather than guessing at the right number of features.

  • Highly complex models lead to overfitting.
  • To reduce overfitting we reduce model complexity, that is, reduce the number of redundant features contributing to the model.
  • Regularization does this by penalising the weight vector when it gets too large, shrinking it toward zero.

Ridge regularization (L2)

Ordinary least squares chooses

$$\hat w = \arg\min_{w}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\bigl(y_i-\mathbf{x}_i^{\top}w\bigr)^{2}$$

Ridge adds a penalty on the squared size of the weights:

$$J(w)=\sum_{i=1}^{n}\bigl(y_i-\mathbf{x}_i^{\top}w\bigr)^{2}+\lambda\sum_{j=1}^{p}w_j^{2}$$

In matrix form, with \(\lambda\) the regularization parameter:

$$\min_{w}\;\underbrace{\lVert y-Xw\rVert_2^{2}}_{\text{residual sum of squares}}+\lambda\underbrace{\lVert w\rVert_2^{2}}_{\text{penalty}}$$

The derivation runs exactly as in block 4. The penalty contributes \(2\lambda w\) to the gradient, so

$$-2X^{\top}y+2X^{\top}Xw+2\lambda w = 0 \;\Longrightarrow\; \bigl(X^{\top}X+\lambda I\bigr)w = X^{\top}y$$
$$\hat w^{\,\text{ridge}} = \bigl(X^{\top}X+\lambda I\bigr)^{-1}X^{\top}y$$
Why the inverse always exists now

\(X^{\top}X\) is positive semidefinite, so its eigenvalues are all \(\ge 0\). Adding \(\lambda I\) shifts every eigenvalue up by \(\lambda\), making them all \(\ge\lambda>0\). The matrix is therefore invertible unconditionally — even when \(n<d\) and plain OLS has no unique solution at all. Regularization is not only a cure for overfitting; it repairs the closed form itself.

Interactive: geogebra.org/m/vy9zk7js

Lasso regularization (L1)

Same idea, but the penalty uses absolute values rather than squares:

$$J(w)=\sum_{i=1}^{n}\bigl(y_i-\mathbf{x}_i^{\top}w\bigr)^{2}+\lambda\sum_{j=1}^{p}\lvert w_j\rvert$$
$$\min_{w}\;\underbrace{\lVert y-Xw\rVert_2^{2}}_{\text{residual sum of squares}}+\lambda\underbrace{\lVert w\rVert_1}_{\text{L1 penalty}}$$

The absolute value is not differentiable at zero, so there is no closed form — lasso needs iterative methods. That same corner is what makes it set coefficients to exactly zero rather than merely small.

Interactive: geogebra.org/m/s4nwkwpa

The geometry

Ridge versus lasso

PropertyRidge (L2)Lasso (L1)
Shrinks coefficientsYes, but never exactly to zeroYes, and many become exactly zero
Feature selectionNoYes — the solution is sparse
Correlated predictorsSpreads weight across themPicks one, ignores the others
StabilityMore stableLess stable with collinearity
Computational solutionClosed formIterative methods
GeometryCircle / hypersphere constraintDiamond / L1-ball constraint

Shrinkage versus sparsity

Two practical rules

Standardize before regularizing. The penalty depends on the units of each feature, so a feature measured in metres and the same feature in centimetres get penalised completely differently. Plain OLS is immune to this; ridge and lasso are not.

Do not penalise the intercept. Shrinking \(w_0\) toward zero pulls predictions toward zero rather than toward the mean of \(y\), which is not what you want.

As \(\lambda\to\infty\), what happens to the weights, the bias and the variance?

All penalised weights go to zero — ridge asymptotically, lasso exactly. The model becomes a constant prediction, so variance goes to zero and bias becomes as large as it can be. As \(\lambda\to 0\) you recover OLS: lowest bias, highest variance. \(\lambda\) is therefore a direct dial on the bias-variance trade-off from block 12, and its value is chosen by cross-validation from block 13.

Three corrections against the lecture slides. The gradient descent update for linear regression adds the error-weighted sum, because the gradient already carries a minus sign. Squared bias is \((\mathbb{E}[\hat Y]-Y)^2\), with the expectation inside. And in the feature scaling example it is \(x_2\gg x_1\), not the reverse — feature 2 holds the values in the hundreds.
